newsitem.title: USA: Ex-dictator Somoza's pistol gets $5,750 at auction.
newsitem.headline: Ex-dictator Somoza's pistol gets $5,750 at auction.

text.p: An associate of the late Nicaraguan dictator Anastasio Somoza Debayle paid $5,750 for his gold-plated, engraved pistol at an auction in Miami on Saturday as the former strongman's mistress, who says she is now penniless, sat and wept.
High prices were also paid for photograph collections and Somoza government documents and papers on a day of nostalgia for Miami's Nicaraguan exile community.

Claudio Linarte, financial director in a Miami firm, said he bought the revolver because he wanted a memento of Somoza. "I am a proud Nicaraguan," he said. "To have this is a symbol of respect for the president."

Linarte said he had worked for a Somoza financial company before the 1979 Sandinista revolution that ousted him. Other exiles in the crowd of the auction of Somoza memorabilia said he was a former member of the notorious National Guard.

Somoza ruled Nicaragua from 1967 to 1972 then from 1974 until his downfall in 1979. Along the way he amassed a huge fortune, running the impoverished Central American company like a personal fiefdom until fleeing for Miami as the Sandinista guerrilla army closed in on the capital Managua in July 1979.
He reputedly filled his personal coffers with international aid funds donated as relief for a devastating earthquake in 1972.
He was assassinated in 1980 in a bazooka attack in the Paraguayan capital Asuncion, where he was living in exile.
The auctioned goods had been in the possession of his longtime mistress, Dinorah Sampson, who left Managua two days before the dictator's flight.

She told Reuters at the auction she had put the belongings into storage while her house in Coral Gables was refurbished. She lost them when her financial advisers failed to pay three months' storage fees of $1,000 and the warehouse sold them off to a dealer. She will get none of the proceeds.
"This is a sad day for me. I took these things from Nicaragua. They are memories of my life with the president."
Dinorah, dressed in designer clothes and draped in jewelry, said the advisers had squandered all her money.
"They have all my money. The question is where is my money," she said.
Raymond Molina, a lawyer who lobbied the Jimmy Carter administration on Somoza's behalf in the 1970s, said Dinorah was now destitute.
"It is a sad development. It should never have come to this," he said. "She has received many calls of solidarity."
The Astra .38 calibre pistol was the auction highlight. It is gold-plated with a walnut stock and engraved with foliage, doves and the inscription "Unceta y Guernica, Spain."
As it is still in working order, Linarte must collect it from the auction house's designated licensed gun dealer -- "Big Al's Gun and Pawn" of West Hallendale.

Files of government papers and documents went for $1,600 to a telephome bidder. A collection of 81 books from the dictator's personal library sold for $5,500 and a collection of state and ceremonial photographs for $2,300.
A reminder of Somoza's friendship with the U.S. government, a trophy from the infantry school at Fort Benning, Georgia, was sold for $300.
A nephew of Somoza's, Gabriel Traversario Debayle, who unsuccessfully bid for some items, said he believed the phone bidders were Somoza's children.
"I feel for Dinorah. She had a life with the president. What is interesting is the reaction he still gets."
